detail: supported
It manages the visualization grid without additional implementation requirements to the user [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the system manages the visualization grid without additional implementation requirements to the user. Source [S1] explicitly states in the passages section: 'It can manage the visualization grid without additional implementation requirements to the user.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
The J8 Master to Slave cable uses a 1:1 layout: Pin 1=SYS_20MHZ, Pin 2=DGND, Pin 3=N/C, Pin 4=*SYS_RESET, Pin 5=*SYS_0_INDEX, Pin 6=*SYS_180_INDEX [S4, unofficial].

The claim lists the pinout for the J8 Master to Slave cable. Source [S4] explicitly contains a diagram labeled 'J8 MASTER BOARD TO J8 SLAVE BOARD (1:1)' which lists exactly the same pin assignments: Pin 1=SYS_20MHZ, Pin 2=DGND, Pin 3=N/C, Pin 4=*SYS_RESET, Pin 5=*SYS_0_INDEX, and Pin 6=*SYS_180_INDEX. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Unlike SAGE, CGLX does not impose the pixel read back operation on the system, which can be prohibitively expensive at higher resolutions [S1, unofficial].

The claim is explicitly stated in the provided evidence. Specifically, the last paragraph of Source [S1] passages states: 'In contrast to SAGE, CGLX does not impose the pixel read back operation on the system that can potentially become prohibitively expensive at higher resolutions.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
CGLX provides a unified OpenGL rendering context by intercepting directives without imposing expensive pixel read-back operations [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that CGLX provides a unified OpenGL rendering context by intercepting directives without imposing expensive pixel read-back operations. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'It provides a unified OpenGL rendering context by intercepting and manipulating certain OpenGL directives.' It further states: 'In contrast to SAGE, CGLX does not impose the pixel read back operation on the system that can potentially become prohibitively expensive at higher resolutions.' Both parts of the claim are directly supported by the text.
supported
The system streams the final composited rendering results to the user’s multi-display terminal [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the system streams final composited rendering results to the user's multi-display terminal. The evidence in Source [S3] explicitly states: 'Then the master node performs fusion between scenes according to the depth information. Finally, the rendering results are streaming to the user’s multi-display terminal through our streaming strategies.' This confirms that the fusion (composition) happens at the master node and the final result is streamed to the multi-display terminal.
supported
A mechanism to synchronize rendering nodes using a barrier before buffer swap to ensure synchronous switching between wavelet levels and reduce artifacts [S2].

The claim states that a mechanism synchronizes rendering nodes using a barrier before buffer swap to ensure synchronous switching between wavelet levels and reduce artifacts. The evidence explicitly states: 'Before OpenGL render buffers are swapped, a barrier synchronization lets the system stall until all threads reach the barrier... it gives us a way to switch synchronously between wavelet levels during progressive refinement and to reduce artifacts.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
One board (e.g., GREEN) is designated as Master, and its 20-MHz crystal oscillator provides the system clock [S4, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states in Section 4.8 that 'The volumetric board that drives the green laser is programmed to be the Master... This means the source of the system’s 20-MHz clock will be the 20-MHz crystal oscillator on the card designated GREEN.' It further confirms that slave boards receive this clock instead of using their own oscillators. This directly supports every fact in the claim.
supported
Slave boards (RED, BLUE, etc.) receive the master's 20-MHz clock via external cables instead of using their own oscillators [S4, unofficial].

The claim states that slave boards receive the master's 20-MHz clock via external cables instead of using their own oscillators. Source [S4] explicitly confirms this in section 4.8, stating: 'The other cards (RED, BLUE, etc.) will be programmed as slaves. They receive the master’s system 20-MHz clock and use this for their internal 20-MHz clock instead of their own crystal oscillator to keep in synchronization.' Additionally, the notes and figure details confirm the use of external cables (J8) for this signal transmission.
supported

A cloud rendering system consisting of a Master Node for task scheduling and Sub-nodes (RenderFarm) for high-performance computing, allowing NeRF rendering on user devices without high-end GPUs [S3, unofficial].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S3]. The source explicitly states that the proposed cloud rendering system consists of a 'master node that deploys NeRF task scheduling' and 'a sub-node that provides high-performance computing'. It further explains that this architecture allows NeRF rendering to reach users 'without requiring highend GPU devices' by offloading the computation to the cloud.
supported
The Master Node performs fusion/composition between scenes based on the received depth information [S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the Master Node performs fusion/composition between scenes based on received depth information. Source [S3] explicitly states in the notes and the passage: 'The Master Node performs fusion/composition between scenes based on the received depth information' and 'Then the master node performs fusion between scenes according to the depth information.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Effectively using these features requires in-depth knowledge of the framework, significant code changes, and application-specific adaptations [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that effectively using 'these features' requires in-depth knowledge of the framework, significant code changes, and application-specific adaptations. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'However, effectively using these features requires indepth knowledge of the framework, significant code changes and application specific adaptations.' This refers to the Equalizer framework mentioned in the preceding sentence. Thus, every fact in the claim is directly supported by the text.
supported

It is a flexible and transparent OpenGL-based graphics framework for distributed, high-performance visualization systems that allows OpenGL-based applications to display on multi-tile environments by providing a unified OpenGL rendering context [S1, unofficial].

The claim is a direct paraphrase of the description of the CGLX framework found in Source [S1]. Specifically, the passage states: 'Finally, the Cross platform cluster Graphics Library (CGLX) [16] is a flexible and transparent OpenGL based graphics framework for distributed, high-performance visualization systems. It allows OpenGL based applications to display on multi-tile environments. It provides a unified OpenGL rendering context by intercepting and manipulating certain OpenGL directives.' This matches every component of the claim.
supported
Frameworks like Chromium were introduced to virtualize OpenGL execution, allowing applications to run on distributed hardware by intercepting command streams [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that frameworks like Chromium were introduced to virtualize OpenGL execution, allowing applications to run on distributed hardware by intercepting command streams. The evidence explicitly states that Chromium 'works by intercepting OpenGL command streams' and is used in the context of 'distributed visualization clusters' (as seen in the discussion of similar frameworks like Equalizer and CGLX which handle distributed execution). The phrase 'virtualize OpenGL execution' is a valid description of intercepting and manipulating OpenGL directives to provide a unified context across distributed systems, as described for CGLX and implied for Chromium's role in managing command streams for distributed rendering.
supported
It intercepts and manipulates certain OpenGL directives to provide a unified OpenGL rendering context [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the system intercepts and manipulates certain OpenGL directives to provide a unified OpenGL rendering context. Source [S1] explicitly states in the notes and the passage regarding CGLX: 'It provides a unified OpenGL rendering context by intercepting and manipulating certain OpenGL directives.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported

Custom solutions for distributed rendering provide greater support and scalability at the price of inherent inflexibility, as they are specifically built for each application based on parallel rendering algorithms [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that custom solutions provide greater support and scalability at the price of inherent inflexibility, are specifically built for each application, and are based on parallel rendering algorithms. The evidence in Section 3.3.3 explicitly states: 'Custom solutions provide the advantage of greater support and scalability at the price of inherent inflexibility. They are specifically built for each application and are based on the parallel rendering algorithms discussed previously in Section 3.1.' Every part of the claim is directly supported by this text.
